title: The rains begin
hook: Asalha Puja marks the first sermon; the rains retreat starts the next day

segments.voice: Yesterday: Poson, Mahinda and the mango tree, and your line, who brought it. Did you thank someone? Today, the next full moon, and two beginnings, one after the other. Day six hundred eighty-four.

In India, the monsoon doesn't drizzle. It arrives. Roads turn to rivers, fields to mud, and anything walking on the ground, worms, insects, frogs, comes up into the open. In the Buddha's time, wandering teachers of many kinds stopped traveling for these months. Buddhist monks, early on, kept walking. People complained, the Vinaya says: these monks trample the green shoots and crush small creatures. So the Buddha set a rule. Stay in one place for the rains. And the full moon just before the rains carries its own memory, the very first teaching. Today: the rains begin.

Start with the full moon. In the Theravada tradition, the full moon of the month Asalha, usually in July, is the anniversary of the first sermon. Two months after his awakening, tradition says, the Buddha found his five former companions in the Deer Park near Benares, and set the wheel of the teaching in motion: the middle way, the four noble truths. One of the five, Kondanna, understood, the first of them to see it. With that, the tradition says, the three jewels were complete: the Buddha, the teaching, and the community. Thailand, Laos and Cambodia mark the day as Asalha Puja, and in Thailand it's a national holiday. People go to the temple, hear the first sermon chanted, and walk three times around the shrine holding candles. Then, the very next day, the rains retreat begins: Vassa, a word that means rain, and also year, because a monk's seniority was counted in rains. For three lunar months, monks stay in one monastery. Some lay people take up something for the season too: giving up alcohol, keeping more precepts, meditating daily, coming to the temple on every moon day. In Thailand, it's a custom for young men to ordain for one Vassa, as a rite of passage. And for a monastery, it's the quiet season, the time for study and practice, with nowhere to go. There's a gentle wisdom in it. Weather you can't change becomes a season you use.
screen: `THE FIRST SERMON'S FULL MOON.` · `KONDANNA UNDERSTANDS.` · `VASSA: THREE MONTHS IN ONE PLACE.` · then, large: `THE RAINS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin a three-month practice. Sit, and settle. Ask yourself: what could I keep for one season? Something small enough to last. Five minutes of sitting each morning. No phone in bed. One kind message a week. Fewer drinks. Let a few options come, and notice which one feels right, not heroic. Picture yourself three months from now, having kept it. Choose it, quietly, here. The bell holds the time.
The rains begin. Asalha Puja remembers the first sermon on the full moon; the next day, the three-month rains retreat, Vassa, starts. Today's word.
Your line: the rains begin. Today, write down your three-month practice and the date it ends. Day six hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: On Asalha Puja, Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia gather at temples to hear the first sermon and circle the shrine with candles; during the following three-month Vassa, monks stay in one monastery and some lay people take on extra practices.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rains retreat is a kind of vacation for monks.
what it means: it's three months in one place, for practice, and to avoid harming crops and creatures.
what a scholar hears: Asalha Puja as a named national observance is modern; Thailand established it in 1958.

notes: Confirm 'two months after his awakening' for the first sermon (traditional: awakening on Vesak, first sermon on Asalha).

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'two months after his awakening' marked 'tradition says'; Kondanna is now 'the first of them to see it' (SN 56.11) rather than 'the first to follow him'; 'many lay people' to 'some'; Thai one-Vassa ordination framed as a custom.
Vassa start dates differ slightly by tradition and in leap years; the script says 'the very next day' per the outline.
